text: 4 Lecture 4 4.1 Operations on linear transformations Definition 4.1 (Composition of linear transformations). Let T : V → W and S : W → U be linear transformations. The composition ST (or S ◦ T ) of T and S is defined as (ST )(x) = S(T (x)). One can also check that ST : V → U is a linear transformation. Proposition 4.2. Let R, S, T be linear transformations. Whenever the composition in each item is defined, we have (i) R(ST ) = (RS)T (ii) R(S + T ) = RS + RT (iii) (R + S)T = RT + ST (iv) For a ∈ F , a(ST ) = (aS)T = S(aT ) (iv) T ◦ idV = T , idW ◦ T = T Proof. One can directly verify these properties following the definition. Remark 4.3. We note that in general ST ̸= T S since as maps T : V → W and S : W → U one can only be composed in the order ST but not in the order of T S. Even when V = W = U , we do have examples of T, S : V → V such that ST ̸= T S. T = ( 1 0 0 0 ) and S = ( 0 1 0 0 ) . Then ST = ( 0 0 0 0 ) and T S = (0 1 0 0 ) . 4.2 Invertibility and rank-nullity theorem Definition 4.4. Let T : V → W be a linear transformation. T is injective (one-to-one) if T (x) = T (y) implies x = y. T is surjective (onto) if for any y ∈ W there is x ∈ V such that T (x) = y T is invertible (nonsingular) if it is both injective and surjective. An invertible T is called an isomorphism between V and W . V and W are isomorphic if there exists an isomorphism between them. We denote V and W are isomorphic by V ∼= W . Definition 4.5. The kernel (null space) of T is ker T = {x ∈ V : T (x) = 0}. The nullity of T is null T = dim ker T . The image (range) of T is im T = {T (x) : x ∈ V }. The rank of T is rank T = dim im T . 18 Lemma 4.6. Let T : V → W be a linear transformation. Then ker T is a subspace of V and im T is a subspace of W . Proof. Since T (0V ) = 0W , 0V ∈ ker T . Let x, y ∈ ker T , c ∈ F . Then T (x + y) = T (x) + T (y) = 0 + 0 = 0 and T (cx) = cT (x) = 0. Thus x + y ∈ ker T , cx ∈ ker T . Since T (0V ) = 0W , 0W ∈ im T . Let u, v ∈ im T . Then there exist x, y ∈ V such that T (x) = u and T (y) = v. We have u + v = T (x) + T (y) = T (x + y) ∈ im T and cu = cT (x) = T (cx) ∈ im T . Proposition 4.7. We have the following characterization of injectivity and surjectivity of a linear transformation T . (i) T is injective if and only if ker T = {0}. (ii) T is surjective if and only if im T = W . Proof. (i) Since T is injective and T (0) = 0, we have ker T = {0}. Suppose T (x) = T (y). Then by linearity of T , T (x − y) = T (x) − T (y) = 0. Thus x − y ∈ ker T = {0}. Hence x = y. (ii) This is just the definition of surjective. Example 4.8. T : F n → F m, T (x1, . . . , xn)t = (x1, . . . , xr, 0, . . . , 0)t for some 0 ≤ r ≤ min(m, n). We have ker T = {(0, · · · , 0, xr+1, . . . , xn)t : xi ∈ F, r + 1 ≤ i ≤ n} and im T = {(x1, . . . , xr, 0, . . . , 0)t : xi ∈ F, 1 ≤ i ≤ r}. We have null T = n − r and rank T = r. T is injective if r = n. T is surjective if r = m. Proposition 4.9. The following are equivalent: (i) T : V → W is invertible. (ii) There is S : W → V linear such that ST = idV and T S = idW . (iii) T maps a basis into a basis. If any of the above items is satisfied, then the linear transformation S in (ii) is unique. Proof. (i)=⇒ (ii) Since T is both injective and surjective, we can define S(y) to be the unique x such that T (x) = y. It follows from definition that ST = idV and T S = idW . We now show that S is linear. In T (x + y) = T (x) + T (y), we take x = S(u) and y = S(v). Then we have T (S(u) + S(v)) = T S(u) + T (S(v)) = u + v. Composing S on both sides from the left, we get S(u) + S(v) = S(u + v) Similarly we have T (cS(u)) = cT S(u) = cu and composing S on both sides, we have S(cu) = cS(u). (ii)=⇒ (iii) Let v1, . . . , vn be a basis of V . We show that T (v1), . . . , T (vn) is a basis of W . To show that T (v1), . . . , T (vn) is linearly independent, let a1T (v1) + · · · + anT (vn) = 0. We compose S on both sides and use the linearity of S and ST = idV , we have S(a1T (v1) + · · · + anT (vn)) = a1v1 + · · · + anvn = 0 = 0. Since v1, . . . , vn is a basis, we have a1 = · · · = an = 0. Let y ∈ W . Since S(y) ∈ V , there exist a1, . . . , an ∈ F such that S(y) = a1v1 + · · · + anvn. Then y = T S(y) = T (a1v1 + · · · + anvn) = a1T (v1) + · · · + anT (vn). Thus W = span(T (v1), . . . , T (vn)). 19 (iii) =⇒ (i) To show that T is injective suppose T (x) = 0. We write x = a1v1 + · · · + anvn. Then by linearity, a1T (v1) + · · · + anT (vn) = T (x) = 0. Since T (v1), . . . , T (vn) is a basis, a1 = · · · = an = 0. To show that T is surjective, let y ∈ W . Since T (v1), . . . , T (vn) is a basis of W , y = a1T (v1) + · · · + anT (vn) = T (a1v1 + · · · + anvn) ∈ im T . To show uniqueness of S, we assume S1, S2 are two maps satisfying (ii). We consider the composition S1T S2. On one hand, (S1T )S2 = idV S2 = S2. On the other hand S1(T S2) = S1idW = S1. Thus S1 = S2. Definition 4.10. The linear transformation S in (ii) is called the inverse of T and is denoted by T −1. Corollary 4.11. If V ∼= W , then dim V = dim W . Proof. If V ∼= W , then there is an isomorphism T : V → W . By Proposition 4.9 (iii), T maps a basis into a basis and hence dim V = dim W . Lemma 4.12. If T ; V → W and S : W → U are both invertible, then ST is invertible and (ST )−1 = T −1S−1. Proof. We have (ST )(T −1S−1) = S(T T −1)S−1 = SS−1 = idU and (T −1S−1)(ST ) = T −1(S−1S)T = T −1T = idV . The conclusion follows from Proposition 4.9. Theorem 4.13 (First isomorphism theorem). Let T : V → W be a linear transforma- tion. We define ¯T : V / ker T → im T to be ¯T (x+ker T ) = T (x). Then ¯T is a well-defined linear transformation and is an isomorphism. V W V / ker T im T T π ¯T i Proof. We first show that ¯T is well-defined. For any x′ ∈ x+ker T , we have x−x′ ∈ ker T . Then T (x) = T (x′) + T (x − x′) = T (x′). ¯T is linear follows from the linearity of T . If ¯T (x + ker T ) = T (x) = 0 then x ∈ ker T . Thus x + ker T = 0 + ker T . This shows ¯T is injective. For any y ∈ im T , there exists x ∈ V such that T (x) = y. Thus ¯T (x + ker T ) = y. This shows that ¯T is surjective. Hence ¯T is an isomorphism. Corollary 4.14 (Rank-nullity theorem). Let T : V → W be a linear transformation. Then dim V = null T + rank T. Proof. By Theorem 4.13, ¯T : V / ker T → im T is an isomorphism. By we have dim(V / ker T ) = dim im T . By Theorem 3.16, we have dim V −dim ker T = dim(V / ker T ) = dim im T . 20 Corollary 4.15 (Underdetermined system of linear equations). Let T : V → W be a linear transformation and dim W < dim V . Then there is 0 ̸= x ∈ V such that T (x) = 0. Proof. null T = dim V − rank T ≥ dim V − dim W > 0. Corollary 4.16. Let V, W be finite dimensional vector spaces such that dim V = dim W and T : V → W be a linear transformation. Then the following are equivalent: (i) T is an isomorphism. (ii) T injective. (iii) T surjective. (iv) There is S : W → V such that ST = idV . (v) There is S : W → V such that T S = idW . Proof. (i) =⇒ (ii): This follows directly from definition. (ii) =⇒ (iii): By (ii) and Lemma 4.7, we have null T = 0. By Corollary 4.14, we have rank T = dim V = dim W . By Lemma 2.17, im T = V . (iii) =⇒ (i): By (iii) we have rank T = dim W = dim V . By Corollary 4.14, we have null T = 0 and hence ker T = {0}. Thus T is an isomorphism. (i) =⇒ (iv) and (i) =⇒ (v): This follows from Proposition 4.9. (iv) =⇒ (ii): Let x ∈ ker T . Then x = ST (x) = S(0) = 0. Thus ker T = {0}. (v) =⇒ (iii): Let y ∈ W . Then y = T S(y) = T (S(y)) ∈ im T . Thus im T = W . Remark 4.17. The infinite dimensional version of (ii) and (iii) in this Corollary is called Fredholm alternative. It is useful in solving PDEs cf. [1, Chapter 8]. 4.3 Basis, coordinates and matrix representation In Lecture 2, we saw that a finite dimensional vector space is built up by a basis. In this section, we will see that given a basis on a vector space, a linear transformation reduces to a matrix. Lemma 4.18 (Basis and coordinates). Let v1, . . . , vn be a basis of V . Then for every v ∈ V , there exists unique x1, . . . , xn ∈ F such that v = x1v1 + · · · + xnvn. Proof. Since v1, . . . , vn spans V , there exist x1, . . . , xn ∈ F such that x = x1v1 + · · · + xnvn. To show uniqueness we assume that x = y1v1 + · · · + ynvn. Then we have (x1 − y1)v1 + · · · + (xn − yn)vn = 0. Since v1, . . . , vn is linearly independent, x1 − y1 = · · · = xn − yn = 0. Thus xi = yi for all 1 ≤ i ≤ n. Definition 4.19. Let β = (v1, . . . , vn) be a basis of V . We say that (x1, . . . , xn)t is the coordinates of v under the basis and we write [v]β for (x1, . . . , xn)t. Theorem 4.20. Let V be a n-dimensional vector space over F . We define the map ϕβ : V → F n by ϕβ(v) = [v]β. Then ϕβ is a linear isomorphism and ϕ−1 β (x1, . . . , xn)t = x1v1 + · · · + xnvn. 21 Proof. We first show that ϕβ is linear. Let ϕβ(v) = (x1, . . . , xn)t and ϕβ(w) = (y1, . . . , yn)t. Then v+w = (x1+y1)v1+· · ·+(xn+yn)vn and hence ϕβ(v+w) = (x1+y1, . . . , xn+yn)t = ϕβ(v) + ϕβ(w). Moreover, cv = cx1v1 + · · · + cxnvn then ϕβ(cv) = cϕβ(v). Next we show that ϕβ is injective. If ϕβ(v) = ϕβ(w) = (x1, . . . , xn)t, then v = x1v1 + · · · + xnvn = w. Hence ϕβ is injective. Finally we show that ϕβ is surjective. For any (x1, . . . , xn)t ∈ F n we take v = x1v1 + · · · + xnvn. Then ϕβ(x) = (x1, . . . , xn)t. Thus ϕβ is an isomorphism and V ∼= F n. Since ϕβ(v) = (x1, . . . , xn)t implies that v = x1v1+· · ·+xnvn, we see that ϕ−1 β (x1, . . . , xn)t = x1v1 + · · · + xnvn. Lemma 4.21. Let T : V → W be a linear transformations and v1, . . . , vn be a basis of V . Then T is uniquely determined by its values at T (v1), . . . , T (vn). Proof. Let v ∈ V . Since v1, . . . , vn is a basis of V , we have v = x1v1 + · · · + xnvn. Then T (v) = T (x1v1 + · · · + xnvn) = x1T (v1) + · · · + xnT (vn). Theorem 4.22. Let T : V → W be a linear transformation. Let β = (v1, . . . , vn) be a basis of V and γ = (w1, . . . , wm) be a basis of W .
